changes.summary: A Surrealist Wunderkammer is an ongoing single-gallery exhibition devoted to the observations of human nature from the perspectives of Surrealism, an international art and literary movement started by André Breton, Paul Éluard, and others in France in the 1920s. Featuring more than 200 works, the installation draws from the museum’s collection as well as long-term loans from the de Menil family and the Rock Foundation. The exhibition includes masks, sculptures, musical instruments, photographic and moving-image technologies, paintings, prints, tourist curios, and other objects that informed the imagination, political aesthetic, and varied artistic practices of Surrealism. Originally opening in 1999 with the title Witnesses–A Surrealist Wunderkammer, the exhibition developed out of conversations between anthropologist Edmund S. Carpenter (1922–2011) and his mother-in-law, Dominique de Menil (1908–1997). The first title was a direct reference to wunderkammern (“wonder rooms”) or curiosity cabinets. Popularized in Europe by the 16th century, wunderkammern were storehouses and royal treasuries for displaying collections of art, natural marvels, and other strange or magical items, such as petrified wood or the long tooth of a narwhale. Alluding to these historical displays, circular brass tags engraved with numbers identify the works on view in the gallery. Carpenter’s motivation for the initial exhibition was to “reveal a common intelligence” that connected the collections of Indigenous arts and Surrealism assembled by the de Menil family during the 20th century. “The point—the intelligence—behind this,” he wrote, “is simply that what first appears as disorder, becomes order once the Surrealist vision is grasped.”
